title: New GeoServer RCE exploit chain seen in the wild two days after disclosure
raw_text: Attackers have begun probing a chain of five GeoServer vulnerabilities that enables unauthenticated remote code execution, just two days after the open source geospatial server project disclosed the flaws. Security firm watchTowr, which operates a global network of honeypot servers, reported that it observed the probing activity in the early morning hours of Wednesday. Attackers from multiple IP addresses created stored queries on GeoServer instances, checked whether they were created, and deleted them immediately, a technique that confirms a server is vulnerable without delivering a malicious payload. GeoServer is widely used by government agencies, utilities, and large organizations to publish maps and geospatial data, and it has become a recurring target for attackers. The full RCE chain was reported to the project in August by Jonah Burgess, a senior security researcher at Rapid7 who uses the online handle CryptoCat. The GeoServer project shipped fixes in October and early November but only disclosed the vulnerabilities and published advisories for them on Monday. Chained together, the flaws allow an external unauthenticated attacker to bypass security restrictions, read stored secrets, forge an administrator authentication cookie, and ultimately execute code on the underlying host. They affect GeoServer versions 3.0.0 to 3.0.1, 2.28.0 to 2.28.5, and 2.27.6 and earlier. Users are advised to upgrade to the fixed versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7 depending on which major release they use. A five-flaw chain According to Burgess’ technical write-up this week, one flaw (CVE-2026-129244) uses an overly long stored-query request to trigger a filesystem error that exposes the server’s data-directory path. A second flaw (CVE-2026-129243) allows attackers to call services with a slash in their names, such as x/WFS, bypassing access rules and letting unprivileged users create and delete stored queries, an action normally reserved for administrators. A saved query can then read files from the server, returning the administrator’s password digest along with a cookie-signing key that ships with the default value “geoserver,” a bug tracked as CVE-2026-120705. That key can then be used to forge an administrator cookie (CVE-2026-129245), and a deserialization bug in the database-backed user service finally allows running code with the privileges of the GeoServer process (CVE-2026-129242). Only the final step results in code execution, and only one of the five flaws, the predictable signing key, is rated as critical. Burgess also published a proof-of-concept exploit for the chain. However, researchers from Eye Security independently found a shorter, three-flaw RCE chain that shares the file-read step but reaches code execution through a different bug tracked as CVE-2026-120704 that was also patched. Eye Security used AI models to find the bugs, and the fact that different researchers found some of the same vulnerabilities (two researchers named McCaulay and Quikko are also credited on some of the flaws) highlights the fact that attackers could use AI to find the flaws as well, especially since patches can serve as blueprints for AI agents . In fact, Eye Security had to consider whether delaying disclosure after patches were released was worth the risk of malicious actors finding them independently in the meantime. “We used AI to find these bugs, and a determined attacker with good models could do the same, especially with the official patch to diff against,” Niels Teusink, a security researcher at Eye Security, wrote this week. “That makes the gap between releasing a fix and publishing details riskier than it used to be.” After the advisories were published, it took less than two days for attackers to start probing the flaws to identify vulnerable servers, likely in preparation for attacks. Over 3,000 GeoServer instances are currently exposed to the internet. GeoServer keeps getting targeted This is not the first time GeoServer has been targeted by attackers. In August , a zero-day SQL injection flaw was exploited before a patch was available , and in December 2025 the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) ordered US agencies to patch another GeoServer flaw under active exploitation . Upgrading to a patched release resolves the entire chain, but the patches generate a new cookie-signing key that invalidates existing remember-me sessions. Clustered deployments must set a shared GEOSERVER_REMEMBERME_KEY so nodes sign cookies with the same key, and since the data directory might have been exposed, administrators should also change their passwords. Where patching cannot happen immediately, GeoServer advises blocking requests whose service value contains a slash, removing the remember-me filter from the web filter chain, and checking the data directory’s wfs/query folders for stored queries not created by a legitimate user.

title: Palo Alto confirms Fragnesia exploitation against firewalls in PHP2Shell attacks
raw_text: Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that attackers exploited Fragnesia, a Linux kernel flaw, to gain root on PAN-OS firewalls through the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, and has shipped fixes six months after the bug was patched in Linux. The vulnerability allows a locally authenticated, low-privileged attacker to escalate privileges to root. “Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet,” the company said in its November 25 security advisory. It added that all observed attacks targeted devices whose management interface “is exposed to the internet, a configuration our best practices advise against.” Even so, the company labeled the bulletin “Informational” and gave it no CVSS score. Fixed builds span every supported PAN-OS branch from 10.2 to 12.2. A second patch cycle in a month For PAN-OS customers, these are the second set of hotfixes in a month. Between October 25 and October 29, Palo Alto released fixes for PHP2Shell, according to the timeline in its PHP2Shell advisory . PHP2Shell is the collective name for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical flaws in the PHP runtime behind the PAN-OS management web interface. The company rated both flaws 9.2 on CVSS 4.0, and the advisory, which covers PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama, said, “active exploitation has been observed.” The October builds do not include the kernel fix, which arrives in later releases listed in the new bulletin. Even for customers who have patched PHP2Shell, Palo Alto said in the bulletin that it “still recommend[s] upgrading to a fixed release at your next maintenance interval.” Palo Alto is relaxed about the timing. “If you are running a fixed PAN-OS listed in the CVE-2026-109618 advisory, you are protected,” the bulletin said. “The only known way to exploit this vulnerability requires an attacker to first exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerability,” it added. For devices with management access restricted to trusted internal IP addresses, it advises upgrading “at your next maintenance interval.” Duncan Brown, group vice president and global domain lead for worldwide security and trust at IDC, said that the approach is defensible when vulnerabilities are chained. “It’s acceptable to apply one patch that effectively breaks the chain. Ideally, all vulnerabilities would be patched as early as possible, but in many cases this is not practical,” Brown said. Rahul Karne, a senior digital forensics and incident response analyst, called patching PHP2Shell a reasonable short-term step, but said it blocks the known way in without fixing the bug. “The key word is ‘known,’” Karne said. He pointed out that public exploit code for Fragnesia, including a Metasploit module, is available, and that any other code execution flaw on the device would make the kernel bug usable again. From web shell to root The chain has been public for almost a month. In late October, Dream Security researchers reported that attackers combined PHP2Shell with Fragnesia to compromise firewalls running vulnerable PAN-OS builds. According to Dream, the attackers used PHP2Shell to run code as the web service account and then used the kernel flaw to become root. From there, they tunneled into internal networks and stole credentials, private keys, and network topology data. The kernel bug itself is not new. William Bowling, a researcher at Zellic, disclosed Fragnesia on May 13 along with a proof-of-concept exploit and an upstream kernel patch, after finding it with the help of the company’s V12 AI auditing agent. Fedora shipped a fixed kernel the next day. Karne said some delay is normal for appliance vendors that maintain custom kernels across many hardware models, but 195 days is too long when exploit code is public. Customers should hear whether they are affected within a week of such a disclosure and get a fix within about 30 days, he said. “A firewall should not get security fixes more slowly than the servers it protects,” Karne said. The firewall as a foothold Palo Alto is not the only security vendor whose appliances were rooted this way. In November, Check Point said “a couple of dozen” customers were hit after attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Gaia OS privilege escalation flaw to take over gateways and deploy a wiper. Niyati Daftary, principal analyst at Gartner, said CISOs should treat the incident as a weakness in their trust model for security appliances, not merely a patching issue. “A firewall running Linux, PHP and other third-party components must be assessed with the same rigor as any privileged, internet-facing server,” Daftary said. “Vendor labels such as ‘Informational’ should never override enterprise risk analysis when flaws can be chained to achieve root access.” “If a device is exposed during the attack window, merely applying the hotfix does not establish trust,” she added. Teams should review administrative access, rotate credentials and certificates, hunt for persistence, and reimage the appliance from a known-good build when root compromise cannot be ruled out, she said. Asked why the kernel fix took six months to reach PAN-OS, and whether Panorama is affected, Palo Alto said it had “no further information to share beyond what is outlined in the advisory at this time.”

It added that all observed attacks targeted devices whose management interface “is exposed to the internet, a configuration our best practices advise against.” Even so, the company labeled the bulletin “Informational” and gave it no CVSS score.

title: Broadcom issues fixes for 23 new VMware flaws, three critical
raw_text: Broadcom on Tuesday reported almost two dozen new security vulnerabilities in VMware, adding to a lengthy list of fixes from this month alone. The most serious of the flaws in the current advisory is a vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, CVE-2026-123903, assigned a CVSSv3 base score of 9.8 (Critical). “A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system,” it said. In a supplemental document accompanying the alert , Broadcom noted that because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing, the advisory comes just two days before the US Thanksgiving holiday, admitting, “this timing is not optimal.” The company said that the advisory covers a total of 23 issues, seven of which are in vCenter: an authentication bypass and three denial-of-service issues in the VMware Directory Service, an arbitrary file write while processing certain archives, a local privilege escalation in a vpxd service script, and a security policy enforcement failure in the vSphere Distributed Switch (vDS). Seven more are in ESX: a heap out-of-bounds write and a use-after-free in the I/O filter service, an out-of-bounds write in the Extensible Host Controller Interface (XHCI) USB controller, a stack-based buffer overflow in the VMkernel, a security bypass in the host configuration store, a signature verification bypass, and a denial of service in guest RPC. The remaining flaws affect VMware Workstation, VMware Fusion, VMware Tools, and VMware Avi Load Balancer. However, the company noted that the fixes delivered to address the flaws in last week’s advisory resolve some of the issues highlighted in the current batch. “If you applied vCenter 8.0 U3m for VMSA-2026-0009 , including on VCF 5.2.x, you do not need to update vCenter again, but vCenter 9.1.x needs the update in this advisory,” Broadcom said. “ESX was not part of VMSA-2026-0009 and needs the update in this advisory. VMSA-2026-0009 also resolved issues in SDDC Manager, which this advisory does not update. If you have not applied the SDDC Manager update from VMSA-2026-0009, apply it separately. This advisory also includes a VMware Tools update. Updating vCenter and ESX does not update VMware Tools inside virtual machines, so plan that update separately.” It added, “if you have a question about whether you are affected, it is likely that you are and should take action immediately.” Difference of opinion on patching urgency So is this a signal to interrupt the US Thanksgiving holiday to address the flaws? Opinions differ. Tyler Reguly , Fortra’s associate director of security R&D, argued that although a 9.8 score is about as high as they get, the nature of the holes might not merit extreme scheduling. There are three vulnerabilities rated 9.8 in severity listed in the current batch, affecting VMware vCenter and ESX. He pointed out, “neither of these [affected] systems should be present on your external interfaces, so the risk would need to be internal. That means we’re talking about an inside threat or a breach that is already underway. These are important vulnerabilities, so there’s no doubt about that, but they are not so important that anyone should interrupt their holiday weekend.” Reguly suggested a strict interpretation of CISA guidance to support his contention that these patches may not merit emergency response. “If we take a look at CISA BOD-26-04 as our guidance on this, is the service publicly exposed? It shouldn’t be, so let’s say no. Is this vulnerability in the KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog]? No. Could it be automated? Unknown, so let’s assume yes for safety’s sake,” he said. “A result of No, No, and Yes translates to line 13 on the BOD-26-04 remediation timelines, which allows for 60 days to fix the issue.” He observed that the recent onslaught of vulnerabilities has made us “a bit like Pavlov’s dog:” We’ve been conditioned to react every time we see CVSS 9.8. “This is a dangerous and potentially harmful conditioning that we need to make every effort to break,” he said. “We need to remind ourselves that the severity of a vulnerability does not reflect risk to an organization, just as the bell did not represent food.” Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, disagreed. He considered the current advisory, VMSA-2026-0011, to be “a big deal because it hits vCenter and ESX, the two systems that run every virtual machine, with flaws that need no password. Skip the patch, and one attacker can take down or take over every virtual machine you run. You are essentially toast. Patch now.” Dickson noted that this batch of alerts contains multiple problematic security issues, which include authentication bypass in vCenter; permitting an attacker with network access to run code on the hypervisor itself; and another bug that lets an administrator inside a virtual machine on Workstation or Fusion run code on the host computer. “Let’s face it: AI loves to chain vulnerabilities,” he said. He is also worried about the large number of VMware patches this month alone, especially those in vCenter. “The frequency of VMware’s vCenter flaws is a concern, as they keep landing in the same place,” he said. “The new flaw is distinct from last week’s. Distinct is not comforting. Three different holes in the same wall is a wall problem.” He pointed out, “The directory service has become vCenter’s Achilles’ heel. This advisory adds three denial-of-service flaws in the same service for good measure.”

title: Digital Realty: PUE hides carbon, and diesel is on the way out
raw_text:
Standard metrics like power usage effectiveness (PUE) and water usage effectiveness (WUE) ignore carbon intensity in the local electricity grid. That means a higher-PUE facility that runs on low-carbon hydro power can be greener than chasing low PUE through water-intensive cooling.

That’s the view of Mauro Leuce, senior director of global design and engineering standards at Digital Realty, who spoke to Computer Weekly at Schneider Electric’s datacentre cooling equipment assembly site in Conselve, Italy.

In the interview, Leuce also spoke about why modern datacentre cooling avoids water loss and treats closed-loop liquid “like gold”. And that changes in datacentre outage protection and grid operator requirements to stay connected mean diesel generators are giving way to batteries on-site.

Why does the way the industry talks about water matter, and what is efficiency really about?

Stating simply that we don’t use water may be counterproductive, because then we lose trust. For me, my very first mission should be creating trust in communities, because if they understand how the datacentre works, that will help both of us.

If I don’t sell efficiencies to my customer, nobody will come to Digital Realty to lease a space, so efficiency is quite an important factor when the customer selects their sites.

Being efficient is one of our top priorities. At the moment, most technologies try to ensure you transfer heat as fast as possible to the outside. What has not been done in a large-scale deployment is to explore what else you can do with heat that has been extracted, such as heat reuse and district heating.

What do customers ask about efficiency, and is PUE the right measure?

At the moment, PUE and WUE are the two parameters that put a facility on a scale from bad to good. However, those two parameters are not the only ones that can give a true indication of how efficient a facility is, because a facility on paper may have a higher PUE, but the carbon intensity of the grid is low, such as in Norway and Finland, for example, because they use a lot of hydroelectric power.

“The cost of purifying liquid in the technology cooling system is so high that the last thing you want is to lose that water or constantly refill. We are using laboratory-grade stainless steel pipework, leak-proof valves, and so on. If there is leakage, it will be a big issue, so water is treated like gold”

Mauro Leuce, Digital Realty

PUE is just a ratio. It’s a number with no unit of measurement, and it’s the ratio between energy used overall and the energy utilised by the IT equipment. So, having as low energy as possible tells you how efficiently that is done.

But I could achieve efficient cooling using water, by evaporative cooling. It’s very efficient because you practically use the water to evaporate and cool down without using any energy. So, there is a trade-off between water and electricity, but it all depends on carbon intensity.

Is anyone building evaporative water-loss systems now?

No, it’s becoming uncommon, mainly because of the cost associated with water treatment. So having water sprayed on the chillers before evaporative cooling requires pH control, acid dosing, etc. Our position in EMEA is you stick with the air-cooled free-cooling chiller and that’s it. There’s no point investing in adiabatic as a plan B or whatever.

What do Digital Realty’s customers actually demand around efficiency in energy and water?

They ask, what is your PUE? What is your WUE? If you use water or not? Because they also have their environmental commitments. I don’t know if you saw that there’s been a Royal Decree mandating 1.15 PUE in Madrid. They are still reconsidering that statement because the only way to achieve those numbers would be to use water, but you don’t want that in a water-stressed region like Madrid.

How much water does a site actually draw?

We only ask for a water connection for our toilets, the sprinkler system, the services to refill the closed loop and whatever. So in reality, our connection is no different than a normal factory. The cost of purifying liquid in the technology cooling system is so high that the last thing you want is to lose that water or constantly refill. We are using laboratory-grade stainless steel pipework, leak-proof valves, and so on. If there is leakage, it will be a big issue. So for us, water is treated like gold, or even more than gold.

How is backup power changing?

That is by contract, depending on the customers. The basic requirement for any datacentre, if you follow the Uptime Institute recommendations, is always 12 hours of fuel storage.

But now customers are starting to ask to change service level agreements, to the point where they will be willing to not have generators on site because they can rely on active-active workloads. That’s where one workload is run in two different facilities at the same time, so that if one datacentre goes down, you still have plan B.

There will still be a portion of generators installed for basic emergency services such as the network room. The network spine needs to be still there for X number of hours, which will be agreed with the customers.

But there is a shift from having on-site generator backup, which was the de facto standard until a few years ago. Now there is a shift to installing battery energy storage systems, with the reason coming from the utility grid requirements.

The grid now asks us to stay connected, even when there are disturbances on the grid, which means we have to continue to operate and stay connected, even if there are very large dips in voltage and frequency.

To do that, the only way is utilising battery energy storage systems called grid-forming [methods to establish and stabilise grid voltage and frequency rather than just passively follow them]. They can control the voltage and stabilise it. Generators are now practically obsolete, because the utility asks us to stay connected, when usually before we were disconnecting and going generator-only.

title: Resilience takes centre stage as applications move to the edge
raw_text:
Real-time digital services succeed or fail on the basis of the digital experience. As consumers, we all know the frustration that comes with a stalled TV show, a video game that crashes mid-stream, or an ecommerce transaction that fails. For businesses the implications can be even more serious, with entire operations grinding to a halt. In both cases - consumer and industrial - disruption to real-time digital services shows up in damaged customer relationships and even lost revenue.

That’s why edge computing is coming to the fore. By running compute and processing data on local servers physically located close to where applications are consumed, enterprises can reduce latency. With data no longer needing to travel to a distant data centre, businesses can deliver content, run applications, and enforce security controls with much higher levels of performance. Edge computing also enables businesses to reduce pressure on central infrastructure and support more personalised and responsive services, among others.

However, the approach also introduces new challenges around visibility, control, and resilience across distributed environments. If organisations are to overcome these challenges, they need to build their edge environments with security and governance baked into the operating model from the get go.

The role of software in scaling edge environments

With digital services increasingly reliant on real-time decision-making - a trend that agentic AI will massively accelerate - businesses will need to scale their edge infrastructure sustainably and cost-effectively.

“Brute force” expansion will not achieve the desired result. Businesses that attempt to meet growing demand for real-time services by continually expanding their infrastructure footprint will find their costs quickly become unsustainable. Meanwhile, the edge network will become unmanageably complex, while energy use shoots through the roof and the number of potential points of failure proliferate. 

Thinking of edge only in terms of hardware is to miss the point entirely. True value stems from putting in place software-driven infrastructure, as this provides enterprises with the ability to apply logic, route traffic, enforce policy, and process data closer to users, while still operating with consistency across regions and environments.

Rather than simply building more infrastructure, the right software layer enables organisations to use their existing systems more efficiently, with software making decisions about where workloads run, how traffic moves, and what happens when systems degrade.

This capability is going to become even more important as AI accelerates the adoption of hybrid infrastructure. According to recent research from Foundry, 66% organisations have moved or plan to move applications or workloads out of the public cloud to on-premises or colocation locations. In these increasingly complex enterprise networks, software-driven control becomes non-negotiable.

Tying governance to workloads

As the edge transforms where workloads run, enterprises need to adapt their governance controls. Currently, policies around factors including data handling, access, compliance, and security are designed for a centralised architecture where workloads are confined to the data centre. Clearly, businesses shifting workloads to the edge need to ensure that their policies and controls are brought along for the ride. Governance should be inextricably linked to the workloads they control, and applied to wherever these workloads run.

In practice, enterprises need to be able to identify 1) what datasets are being processed where, 2) who has the ability to change governance rules, and 3) how changes to rules are monitored. This governance foundation is absolutely critical to ensuring that distributed infrastructure is compliant with regulatory and internal mandates and easy to manage.

Protecting the customer experience through resilience

Highly centralised infrastructure brings with it inherent risk. Organisations are in effect putting all their eggs in a single basket. An outage in one region or department can bring down all dependent systems simultaneously. There’s less flexibility and fewer workarounds.

Decentralised edge servers can reduce that risk by compartmentalising outages and limiting their impact. However, to deliver in full resilience needs to be planned for and included as a design goal from the start. For example, by building intelligence into network design, edge systems can route traffic away from infrastructure that’s experiencing service issues and ensure that content is delivered as fast and seamlessly as possible. Businesses also need to ensure that they have complete visibility of their infrastructure so they can respond rapidly to issues before they impact customers.

Resilience and distributed decision making are vital to edge deployments. These features ensure that infrastructure continues functioning with the lowest possible latency even when things go wrong. They thereby protect real-time services and the revenue and trust that depends on them.

AI makes the edge a business priority

Agentic AI is going to increase demand for real-time digital services over the next five years and provide significant opportunities for growth. In ecommerce, for example, AI agents are already being used to help people search for products, compare prices, and even make purchases. Agentic AI opens a new route to customers and promises new business models, but it also increases the need for robust performance and security capabilities.

When it comes to performance, agents need to be able to operate in real time. Consumers will quickly lose patience if AI systems take too long to return information or carry out tasks. From a security perspective, retailers will need to come up with new ways to distinguish legitimate agents from illegitimate systems designed to scrape data, abuse services, or overwhelm systems. They must maintain a careful balance. While organisations need to ensure the safety of their systems and customer data (which will often include financial data), they must also be careful not to build their defensive walls so high that they block legitimate agents and potentially stop sales.

The edge can help by providing localised infrastructure where businesses can manage agentic interactions before they reach core systems. Applying identity access management controls on local servers, enterprises can verify trusted agents and protect their applications without adversely affecting latency or performance.

The same holds true for businesses assembling digital experiences from separate services for features like search, product information, payments, and personalisation. For customers, these are all part of a single, unified journey, and any delays between services can undermine this experience. The edge brings delivery, application logic, and security closer to the point of use, helping businesses roll out fast, secure and personalised experiences at scale.

Edge computing comes of age

Over the next five years demand for edge processing is going to explode due to agentic AI, richer digital experiences, and rising user expectations, putting unprecedented pressure on enterprise infrastructure. Enterprises that prioritise performance, security, governance, and resilience into their edge builds will be best placed to absorb this pressure and benefit from the opportunities on offer.

Edge computing provides businesses with a platform for growth, and will determine the pace at which enterprises can innovate and scale new real-time digital services. With security and governance hardwired directly into the architecture from day one, businesses will be able to move at speed, protect their infrastructure and data, and outcompete their peers. Meanwhile, consumers will benefit from first-class real-time experiences they can trust.

title: Young British men lose £11bn in the ‘Moneysphere’
raw_text:
Nearly half of young men in the UK have lost a combined total of £11bn through investment scams pitched to them via social media, a survey commissioned by Starling Bank has found.

According to the survey of over 2,000 Gen Z males in the UK, aged between 14 and 29, 44% have fallen for these scams.

Over two million Gen Z men in the UK fell victim to investment scams with an average of just over £5,000 lost, taking the total to about £11bn.

In contrast, 34% of Gen Z females were caught out, according to the survey, which was carried out by Censuswide for Starling Bank.

‘Moneysphere’

Starling refers to this as the “Moneysphere”, which it said is anonymous social media accounts, influencers and artificial intelligence (AI) creators selling get-rich-quick dreams. It includes hyped-up stocks and “risk-free” deals hiding the downsides.

Young men are the main target and are being bombarded with investment tips, with three-quarters pitched investments through social media multiple times a day. Starling’s own customer data shows the same trend towards young men being targeted, with 18-24-year-olds 1.64 times more likely than the average customer to be a victim of this type of scam.

Bernadette Smith, chief customer and banking officer at Starling Bank, said: “The Moneysphere is an increasingly powerful force threatening young men. Social media algorithms are consistently pushing younger consumers into dangerous echo chambers of unregulated financial advice, where extreme risk is normalised.

“Starling urges all UK consumers to take a step back when presented with any investment opportunity, look out for red flags, and question anything that feels too good to be true.”

Rapper and campaigner Professor Green, who has featured in a documentary short speaking with victims of the Moneysphere, said: “It’s easy to see why more and more young men are falling for these social media investment scams – who wouldn’t want to live a life of luxury with just a few clicks?

“However, many young people are being sold a lie – and being targeted by financial advice that is plain wrong at best and illegal at worst. The Moneysphere is a very modern issue, fed by social media being such a personalised experience. Once you watch something, you’ll see much more of it, and for young people trying to improve their financial positions, this could be dangerous – particularly without someone in your corner to stop you from taking the wrong path.”

Wider problem

But it is not just young men falling victim to investment scams. According to a survey by National Trading Standards, 47% of UK adults struggle to tell what online offers are genuine or AI fakes. It also found that 24% feel “overwhelmed” by increasingly sophisticate scams.

The government agency launched its AI Scam Watchlist in September, “revealing the tools and techniques increasingly being used by criminals to supercharge their scams – from digital humans and cloned voices to deepfakes and AI-generated images – and setting out how consumers can protect themselves”.

In August, a survey by TSB found that an average of £3,000 was lost as a result of financial investment fraud via social media platforms.

The findings also revealed that over half of people who followed financial advice from social media platforms lost an average of £700, with 56% of them losing money.

The 25-34 age group were most likely to act on financial advice on social media and use AI for advice, according to the survey. Half of this group have done so in the past year, with 27% using it for advice on savings and 18% for investments.

title: Datacentre water debate blasted for ‘25-year-old assumptions’
raw_text:
Datacentres are routinely cast as water-guzzlers, but that reputation rests on newspaper articles written a quarter of a century ago. Modern facilities are closed-loop and use almost no water. Meanwhile, racks are hotter than ever, but water is being engineered out.

That’s according to executives from Digital Realty and Schneider Electric at the latter’s datacentre event in Conselve, Italy, this week (pictured above), where specialists explained how artificial intelligence (AI) has changed the physics of cooling and what that means for water.

Power draw densification is the backdrop. Andrew Bradner, who leads Schneider’s cooling business, said the average rack wattage in most datacentres had barely moved for 15 years, and hovered at between 8kW (kilowatts) and 12kW. That changed with AI silicon. Nvidia’s H100 pushed racks to 40kW to 80kW, while Blackwell, its successor, takes them past 100kW.

The consequence, said Mauro Leuce, senior director for the global design and engineering standards team at Digital Realty, is that the datacentre data hall itself becomes part of the machine.

“Nowadays, we are not creating a room that cools computers, but actually the room is becoming the computer,” said Leuce. “So we are going back to the 1950s, where IBM had computers which were actually the size of a room.”

Schneider is betting on that trend. At Conselve, its largest cooling manufacturing site in Europe, it is doubling production capacity for coolant distribution units (CDUs) from January 2027 and raising big-chiller output by 50% by the end of 2026, following last year’s acquisition of Motivair. A new test laboratory, due in December 2027, will triple testing capacity and validate chillers up to 4MW (megawatts), Motivair CDUs up to 5MW, and CRAH and fan-wall systems up to 800kW.

“Nowadays, we are not creating a room that cools computers, but actually the room is becoming the computer. So we are going back to the 1950s, where IBM had computers which were actually the size of a room”

Mauro Leuce, Digital Realty

“AI is fundamentally transforming the way in which our customers design and operate datacentres. It is creating unprecedented demand for advanced liquid cooling technologies that can support increasingly powerful computing systems,” said Damien Dhellemmes, senior vice-president of the secure power and datacentre business in Europe at Schneider Electric.

“By doubling our liquid cooling manufacturing capacity in Conselve, we’re strengthening our ability to deploy resilient, scalable and energy-efficient AI infrastructure, while bringing critical technologies and expertise closer to our customers in Europe,” he added.

Liquid cooling demands modest

Liquid cooling, however, is not replacing air cooling. “The idea that an AI factory is fully liquid-cooled is utopian,” said Leuce. “It doesn’t exist. First of all, because even if the rack itself is liquid-cooled, there will be a portion of heat dissipated by radiation. On top of that, customers still need a network, storage and everything else,” Leuce added. He put the balance at around “50-50 at this stage”.

The water question is where the panel was most pointed. Leuce drew the distinction between closed-loop liquid cooling and the evaporative cooling towers of the past.

“We are talking about a liquid coolant, which is no different than what you have in a radiator in a car engine. The radiator cools the engine with a closed loop of liquid coolant that constantly recirculates,” he said. “Liquid cooling has always been in existence. When NASA landed on the moon, all the computers were actually liquid cooled. It’s nothing new.”

The volume of fluid needed to fill such a loop is modest, said Leuce. “How much? It’s about the size of a swimming pool. It’s not an enormous amount to fill it because it’s a closed loop.”

The deeper argument is about carbon. “If you really want to have a sensible discussion about water usage, you need to start to talk about carbon intensity,” said Leuce. “We’re talking about the balance between utilising electricity to cool or utilising water to cool.”

Evaporative cooling made sense when the grid was coal-heavy and power was the dirtier input. “Now, 50 years later, you have quite a lot of renewable energy in the grid. At that point it makes sense to use electricity because it’s greener than water.”

No operator chooses water as a first option, he said. “Nobody wants to use water. We try to stay well away from water because it costs money and it’s risky. A datacentre can be shut down if you have a Legionella issue. No datacentre operator wants to use water as a first solution,” Leuce said.

Water brings treatment costs, storage rules and discharge limits. In dense European hubs, he added, “you can’t discharge water in the public sewer – try that in Frankfurt, Paris, Milan, London; it’s impossible”.

Outdated water data

He reserved his sharpest line for where the public perception comes from. “All the searches where people ask how much water is used by datacentres provide answers picked up from newspaper articles from 25 years ago that are still referenced in searches of today,” he said.

Projected efficiency from Schneider’s own analysis brings big numbers. Tuan Hoang, who heads cooling technology and product development at the company, said higher operating temperatures cut the energy spent on cooling itself.

“We see power reduction by 60% of the overhead, from 1.2, 1.3 down to 1.15 to below 1.1 [PUE]. That is a huge opportunity, where we’re able to remove 60% of the overhead to operate these workloads,” he said.

Those are supplier studies, of course, not independent findings, and the water-free case is strongest in temperate Europe. In hotter, drier markets, the power-for-water trade-off can still run the other way.

Datacentre cooling glossary

PUE (power usage effectiveness): Total facility energy divided by the energy the IT equipment uses. A PUE of 1.0 means every watt reaches the servers; 1.2 means 20% extra goes on cooling, power delivery and losses.

WUE (water usage effectiveness): Water consumed per unit of IT energy, usually litres per kilowatt-hour. It captures water use, not the carbon intensity of the grid.

Cooling: Removing the heat that IT equipment produces so chips stay inside their operating range. Air or liquid carries the heat from the servers to the heat rejection step.

Heat rejection: Where the captured heat leaves the building – to outside air through a chiller or dry cooler, or to water.

CDU (coolant distribution unit): The pump-and-heat-exchanger unit in liquid cooling. It circulates coolant to the cold plates on the chips and separates the server (technology) loop from the building (facility) loop.

Chiller: The machine that removes heat from the water loop. Newer units combine refrigerant-based cooling (a compressor circuit) with water-coil free cooling, so they run the compressor only when the outside air is too warm and switch to water cooling when it is cool enough.

title: Investigation underway into DWP cyber incident as services taken offline
raw_text:
The UK’s largest government department, the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), has taken services offline following a cyber incident.

DWP, which administers disability and health benefits, state pensions and child maintenance payments, said it was working with government cyber security specialists to assess the incident.

Downing Street said an investigation was underway to establish what was behind the cyber incident, but it could not rule out a malicious attack.

The prime minister’s spokesperson said it was a “live and ongoing incident” and that there was “currently no evidence of data loss”, adding: “We’re working as quickly as possible to establish the facts.”

The cyber incident was detected yesterday, when services were taken down as a precaution. “There is currently no evidence to suggest that a malicious actor has targeted other government departments,” the spokesperson added.

DWP services offline

DWP said it was working with the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), part of GCHQ, and the Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3), which coordinates responses to government cyber threats and incidents, to investigate and restore services.

“We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution following a cyber incident,” it said. “Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal.”

DWP websites for people claiming pensions, universal credit and personal independence payments (PIP) were impacted this morning. The sites advised people to try again later if online services were not working and provided a list of telephone contacts.

The department has not disclosed the nature of the incident but is advising customers that it would never message them to ask for bank details or to ask them to click on links.

People began reporting problems accessing DWP services late last night, with reports peaking just before 9.00am this morning, according to reports on the Downdetector website, which monitors the availability of online services.

People trying to access their Universal Credit account reported that the site was unavailable, and others said they had difficulties reporting self-employment income.

“We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible to minimise any disruption,” a spokesperson said.

Government needs to address digital weaknesses

Commenting on the incident, Chi Onwurah, chair of the Science and Technology Committee, said today’s disruption was a wake-up call and that people who rely on DWP systems should be able to trust the tech and data underpinning them to be secure and resilient.

“My committee has repeatedly warned that the government cannot achieve its digital transformation of public services without addressing weaknesses in its digital infrastructure and improving standards of data hygiene. Public bodies hold citizens’ data on trust, and that demands the highest standards,” she added.

“Whilst the government has set out a vision for a modern digital state, it needs a credible delivery plan with clear responsibilities, milestones and metrics against which progress can be judged. It also must provide clarity about what happened at DWP, be transparent about any impact on people’s services and data, and set out what it will do to stop this happening again.” 

Department running on old systems

Giving evidence to a select committee in November, a senior civil servant acknowledged that some of DWP’s computer systems were “extremely” old.

Questioned by Patrick Hurley MP, the committee was told that the “security of DWP systems is absolutely paramount given the amount of personal information we have and the amount of money flowing through our systems”.

“Our cyber security and resilience measures are critical and one of the things that keeps a new permanent secretary awake,” the MPs were told.

Commons Work and Pensions Committee chairwoman Debbie Abrahams said it was a “great relief” that benefits and pensions payments had not been affected.

She said DWP had taken swift action to contain any potential further damage from the cyber incident so that service is restored as soon as possible.

“Although this may interrupt some services, this was absolutely the right thing to do,” she added. “It’s critical that the impact on service users from the outage is investigated and analysed so that timely and accurate advice can be given to them.”

In a post on social media, work and pensions secretary Pat McFadden reiterated the government message that some services had been taken offline as a precaution, that regular benefit and pension payments were unaffected, and that customers did not need to take action.

Organisations are required to report breaches of personal data to the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) within 72 hours. However, DWP has not so far reported any breaches.

An ICO spokesperson said: “We are aware of the incident and are engaging with DWP to establish the circumstances and understand what has happened.”

Downing Street said an investigation was underway to establish what was behind the cyber incident, but it could not rule out a malicious attack.

The prime minister’s spokesperson said it was a “live and ongoing incident” and that there was “currently no evidence of data loss”, adding: “We’re working as quickly as possible to establish the facts.”

The cyber incident was detected yesterday, when services were taken down as a precaution. “There is currently no evidence to suggest that a malicious actor has targeted other government departments,” the spokesperson added.

DWP services offline

DWP said it was working with the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), part of GCHQ, and the Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3), which coordinates responses to government cyber threats and incidents, to investigate and restore services.

“We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution following a cyber incident,” it said. “Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal.”

DWP websites for people claiming pensions, universal credit and personal independence payments (PIP) were impacted this morning. The sites advised people to try again later if online services were not working and provided a list of telephone contacts.

title: ICO reprimands Home Office over data inaccuracy in border system
raw_text:
The UK’s data regulator has reprimanded the Home Office for failures to correct inaccurate information held in a border security system.

On 2 October 2024, the Home Office replaced its existing border control information platform with a federated system known as Helios.

Developed in partnership with weapons manufacturer BAE Systems and the UK Border Force, the Helios system ingests and manages border security watchlist data, pulling information from disparate sources into a single dataset that enables border security officers to identify subjects of interest as they travel.

An investigation by the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), however, found that inaccurate information held by the system has led to people being wrongly detained for additional border checks, and that the Home Office did not put in place measures to correct inaccurate information before the system went live.

The regulator noted that, unlike the previous system, which had a dedicated team to correct information inaccuracies in real time, the federated operating model of Helios meant users could not amend records themselves, and instead had to report issues to the owner of the original source data, who could then correct the data.

On top of having no dedicated measures in place to correct data inaccuracies, the ICO said staff were also told by the Home Office not to include personal information in their rectification requests, making it “virtually impossible” to correct a person’s record because they did not have the necessary information.

During the ICO’s investigation, the Home Office also acknowledged that staff may not even have reported inaccuracies in the first place, as they did not know how to.

  • UK government defends ‘fundamentally flawed’ eVisa system: The government has rejected a suggestion from the Commons Home Affairs Committee that the electronic visa system should move to a more stable, token-based process, rather than the current error-prone system that relies on real-time database checks

The ICO said the failings were “significant” as they could result in people being wrongly detained, potentially causing psychological distress or other adverse consequences, leading it to issue a formal reprimand on 4 November 2026.

“People must be able to trust that decisions about their immigration status at the UK border are made with accurate, up to date information. They also have the right to expect that when information is inaccurate, there is a swift and efficient way for it to be corrected,” said ICO investigations manager Joanne Stones, adding that the Home Office failed to provide staff with a clear, effective process for reporting and correcting inaccurate personal information.

“That failure could potentially have resulted in serious consequences, including people being wrongly detained for additional checks or refused entry to the UK. Data protection by design is not just about the technology. It’s about making sure the processes, responsibilities, training and safeguards needed to protect people's information are correct from the start.”

The problems with Helios were also present from the outset. The ICO noted that, in the first nine days of Helios going live in October 2024, Home Office staff wrongly sent 87 data rectification requests to the team previously responsible for correcting errors in the old system, even though that team was unable to correct the relevant records after Helios’s introduction.

The regulator confirmed that, after introducing a temporary system to allow border officers to report inaccurate information in late October 2025, more than 6,500 incidents were raised by March 2026. In that time, around 5,000 incorrect records were removed.

Stones welcomed these steps taken by the Home Office, adding that while the ICO recognises that federated systems like Helios present unique challenges, the department “must ensure that its permanent solution provides a robust and effective way to identify and correct inaccurate information without delay”.

Commenting on the reprimand, a Home Office spokesperson said: “We take data protection extremely seriously. That is why we have co-operated fully with the Information Commissioner’s Office. 

“We immediately removed all outdated records to minimise delays to passenger journeys and strengthened mechanisms to speed up updates,” they said. “Our processes will continue to be kept under review, ensuring we meet data protection obligations while protecting border security.”

In a blog published on 8 October 2026, BAE Systems described Helios as a “game-changer” and “an example of best practice for delivering complex digital change at national scale”.

It added that since launch, the system “has reduced the need for unnecessary checks by frontline officers, and this has improved efficiency, speed, accuracy and reliability, critically operating 24/7 all with no outages reported in its first year of operation”.

Wider data accuracy issues

This is not the first time the ICO has found issues with data accuracy in Home Office systems.

In one case exclusively reported on by Computer Weekly in June 2025, technical errors with data held by the Home Office in its error-prone electronic visa (eVisa) system were so severe that the regulator found there had been a breach of UK data protection law.

Speaking with Computer Weekly, the person affected said ongoing technical errors with the eVisa system meant his account continued to display an expired student visa, instead of his new spouse visa, and wrong passport information for almost half a year.

Given that millions of people are now required to prove their immigration status via the eVisa system, even a 1% error rate would mean tens of thousands of people are affected at the very least.

Although the Home Office is yet to publish comprehensive information about the exact scale of software errors with its eVisa system, what little evidence is already available indeed suggests tens of thousands have already been affected.

However, despite widespread data issues with the eVisa system being flagged to the ICO by Computer Weekly, civil society groups and the Home Office’s own data, the regulator is yet to take any action over the system.

Computer Weekly contacted the ICO about whether it will formally investigate the eVisa system given the clear issues around data accuracy.

An ICO spokesperson said: “We are actively engaging with the Home Office on matters relating to immigration activities, in line with the memorandum of understanding [MoU] between the ICO and HM Government. The MoU provides a framework for ongoing cooperation and information sharing while preserving the ICO’s independent regulatory role and ability to hold the government to account.”

title: Why AI infrastructure spend fails when IT skips workload checks
raw_text:
The costliest AI infrastructure decision isn't necessarily buying too much. It can also be investing in the wrong capabilities. More storage capacity won't resolve every performance issue, just as specialist hardware won't be necessary for every AI application. 

For UK businesses, these decisions are becoming more important as AI adoption accelerates. According to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), 35% of UK businesses with 10 or more employees now use AI, up from just 12% in late 2023. And with 60% of businesses using AI to streamline and improve operations, attention is shifting from adoption to impact. But translating this momentum into business returns requires a fair bit more than ambition.

The starting point is understanding what the business actually needs. This isn't about buying new kit “off the shelf” for its own sake, but finding solutions that work with your people, your ways of working, and the existing technology estate. New infrastructure investment will be essential for some AI workloads, but business leaders should first assess their current systems to identify where upgrades will deliver the greatest value. Hybrid AI and consumption-based models can also help businesses build on existing infrastructure while introducing new capabilities where needed.

Start with the workload

Lenovo research found that just 41% of IT decision-makers across EMEA feel ready to integrate AI effectively. Improving that readiness begins by establishing what your business wants to achieve. The infrastructure needed to support AI can look very different depending on those ambitions, which is why it's important to start with the workload and assess its requirements, from computing power and storage to data access and security. For example, training a large-scale AI model may require specialist high-performance infrastructure, while an AI-powered knowledge assistant places different demands on secure data access and integration with existing systems. The mistake is assuming that both workloads need the same infrastructure, when one may demand significant new investment and the other could be supported by systems already in place.

An AI readiness assessment can help determine whether their infrastructure can meet the requirements of different workloads, where improvements and investment may be needed, and how those needs could change over time. Even an application that runs comfortably on existing infrastructure during a pilot may expose limitations when deployed across thousands of employees. The key is to assess not just what infrastructure can support today, but whether it can keep up as usage and data demands grow.

Make storage part of the assessment

Storage is a good example of why AI readiness should begin with an assessment rather than an upgrade. Our findings show that 90% of IT decision-makers across EMEA expect AI to drive massive data growth, putting greater focus on whether existing storage infrastructure can meet shifting demands. Businesses may assume they need to replace storage systems or move data into new environments, but the real question is whether their current infrastructure can deliver the performance, accessibility, security and scalability that each workload requires.  

More than ever, enterprise AI solutions depend on timely and reliable access to growing volumes of structured and unstructured data. This might be scanned invoices, say, rather than figures in a database. When planning infrastructure upgrades, it's common to focus on GPU selection, but an undersized or poorly-matched storage solution can increase model-loading times and delay data-intensive operations. Crucially, needing more storage capacity isn't the same as needing better storage performance. Adding capacity won't solve a performance bottleneck caused by slow data access, while more demanding AI workloads may require faster storage to deliver the performance needed at scale. 

For example, a business may have ample storage capacity but still struggle to deliver the throughput needed to feed data-intensive AI workloads, leaving expensive compute resources waiting for data. AI inference and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which pull relevant information from external knowledge sources to inform AI-generated responses, depend on predictable latency and reliable access to models and data. Computer vision requires a solution that can read large amounts of data quickly. 

A hybrid approach to AI can offer greater flexibility in how businesses manage different workloads. For example, organisations may choose to run data-sensitive applications on-premises, use cloud infrastructure for workloads with fluctuating demands, or process information locally on devices where speed is critical. This allows businesses to match infrastructure to the needs of each application, rather than adopting a single approach across their entire AI estate.

Scale investment to demand

For UK businesses looking to scale AI while managing competing spending priorities, financial flexibility is just as important as choosing the right infrastructure. An organisation testing its first AI applications may have very different storage needs from one deploying AI across multiple departments. Committing to significant additional capacity upfront could therefore mean paying for infrastructure long before it is needed.

Consumption-based models offer one way to manage this uncertainty, allowing businesses to expand infrastructure as demand grows rather than committing to large upfront purchases. This can help with avoiding overprovisioning while aligning infrastructure costs more closely with actual usage. However, the priority should be assessing how workloads are likely to develop and choosing an investment approach that balances performance, cost, and future demand. The aim isn't simply to spend less on infrastructure, but to ensure that every investment supports a genuine business need.

From experimentation to success

As AI moves from experimentation into everyday business operations, infrastructure decisions will play a bigger role in managing costs and supporting AI at scale. For IT leaders, the challenge is understanding what their existing infrastructure can support and where additional investment is genuinely needed. The businesses that get this right won't necessarily be those investing the most in AI infrastructure, but those making informed decisions about how to get more from what they already have and where upgrades will deliver the greatest value.

title: The fastest storage server you can deploy is the one that already exists
raw_text:
Enterprise storage planning has traditionally followed a predictable pattern – assess future capacity, specify new hardware, place an order and wait for delivery. But when standard systems take weeks to arrive and specialist configurations can take several months, that process becomes a barrier to the business.

If a capacity expansion depends on equipment that will not arrive for two quarters, the organisation no longer has a procurement inconvenience. It has an operational problem.

Cost pressures make the situation more difficult. NAND prices are rising, premium media is subject to restricted availability and enterprise SSD contract prices increased by 53%-58% in the first quarter of 2026. Memory-dependent purchases are also carrying premiums of 30%-60% over 2024 prices. Organisations are therefore being asked to spend more on infrastructure while potentially waiting much longer to receive it.

Refurbished enterprise hardware offers another option. These systems are already manufactured, tested and held in inventory, allowing many configurations to ship in days rather than months. They can also cost 30%-70% less than equivalent new equipment.

The question is whether second-life hardware can be trusted with production workloads. The answer is, with the right storage architecture, it can.

Hardware flexibility starts with software

Software-defined storage separates the storage platform from the underlying server hardware. Instead of depending on a proprietary appliance or tightly-controlled configuration, organisations can run storage across standard servers from different suppliers and generations.

If a preferred server is unavailable, a business can deploy an alternative configuration from existing inventory and incorporate newer equipment later. Infrastructure projects no longer need to remain on hold while teams wait for one precise model or component.

Mixed-generation environments can form part of a deliberate strategy in which hardware is introduced and retired gradually according to capacity, performance and operational requirements. This allows businesses to buy what is available, extend the useful life of existing equipment and avoid disruptive replacement cycles.

Resilience should not depend on perfect hardware

The most common concern about refurbished equipment is that components with a previous working life may fail sooner than factory-new alternatives.

That concern is reasonable, but any architecture that depends on every drive or server continuing to operate perfectly will eventually encounter problems, regardless of whether the hardware was purchased new or refurbished.

Distributed storage assumes that individual components will fail and protects data across multiple drives and servers using techniques such as replication and erasure coding. When a component becomes unavailable, the system can rebuild protected data across the remaining infrastructure while applications continue operating.

Durability therefore comes from the design of the overall platform rather than the reliability of one device. At sufficient scale, the loss of an individual server becomes a routine operational event rather than a crisis.

The important question is not simply whether a server is new, it is whether the storage architecture has been designed to tolerate its eventual failure.

Faster expansion without permanent lock-in

Refurbished hardware can provide a practical bridge when an organisation urgently needs capacity but still intends to purchase new systems.

Rather than delaying an entire project, teams can introduce available equipment immediately and add newer servers when supply improves. A genuinely hardware-independent platform should allow both to operate within the same environment.

This gives infrastructure teams greater control over when they expand, which suppliers they use and how they allocate budgets. It also reduces the risk that one manufacturer’s availability determines the timetable for a wider business initiative.

Reuse delivers a sustainability benefit

Extending the life of enterprise hardware also supports sustainability objectives.

A significant proportion of a server’s environmental impact is created during manufacturing. Reusing equipment reduces demand for new production while delaying the point at which working technology becomes electronic waste.

For organisations addressing Scope 3 emissions, hardware reuse can complement efforts to improve energy efficiency. It turns circular-economy principles into a practical infrastructure decision rather than treating sustainability solely as a reporting exercise.

In this case, the faster and more economical option may also be the more sustainable one.

Ask different procurement questions

Before accepting a long lead time for a storage expansion, infrastructure leaders should ask:

●     Is the storage platform independent of a particular hardware vendor or generation?

●     Can it accommodate different configurations within one environment?

●     Does its resilience model assume individual components will fail?

●     Could refurbished equipment meet the immediate capacity and performance requirement?

●     What would deployment in weeks rather than quarters mean for the business?

Refurbished hardware will not suit every workload. Equipment must still be sourced responsibly, tested properly and matched to the required performance profile.

However, dismissing it simply because it has had a previous life overlooks how modern storage systems are designed. When resilience is delivered by software and hardware flexibility is built into the architecture, organisations gain another credible route to capacity - without allowing constrained supply chains to dictate the pace of their plans.

Paul Speciale is chief marketing officer and chief technology evangelist at Scality.

title: Independent review into ICO amid claims of ‘toxic culture’ at data protection watchdog
raw_text:
Barrister Karon Monaghan KC has been appointed to conduct an independent review of the UK’s information and data protection regulator, following an internal investigation into its former chief, John Edwards, who resigned after being accused of using “vulgar and highly sexualised language” towards women.

Monaghan – an experienced barrister who has been involved in investigations into sexual harassment at the GMB trade union and the Labour Party’s handling of sexual harassment complaints and antisemitism – is due to report back in the first quarter of next year.

She confirmed today that the Information Commission will not enforce any non-disclosure agreements signed by current and former members of staff at the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), so that there would be no restriction on people speaking, writing or providing documents to the review team.

The review follows complaints by staff of the existence of a wider toxic workplace culture at the ICO, with a staff survey finding that a high proportion had witnessed bullying, harassment and discrimination.

Wynne Parry, national officer at the FDA union for managers and professionals in public service, said there were continuing problems in the workplace, with former staff confirming to Computer Weekly that the ability of the ICO to regulate effectively had been impacted.

“Poor behaviour including bullying remains a significant concern for our members who work at the commission,” he said. “Our recent survey revealed that 65% of participants reported bullying, harassment and discrimination was a serious problem.”

Lawrence Dunne, industrial officer for the PCS union, based in the North West, told Computer Weekly that workplace problems at the ICO went wider than the former Information Commissioner.

"We have said all along that it wasn't a case of one bad apple. There were wider problems in the ICO, and that's been borne out consistently through feedback from staff, staff surveys, and from cases that we deal with as a union," he added.

He said that there had been a higher-than-usual number of union members witnessing bullying and harassment in the organisation, and that people did not feel safe to speak up.

"The biggest problem is that there are too many people who don't feel psychologically safe to challenge instances of inappropriate behaviour or to use their experience to challenge strategic decisions in the organisation," he added.

The review will focus on the culture, accountability and governance of the ICO, including examining how complaints are raised, assessed and acted upon, but will not have powers to discipline staff or determine misconduct.

Women were ‘shocked and uncomfortable’

Former technology secretary Liz Kendall wrote on LinkedIn following Edwards’ resignation in the summer that “multiple women shared testimony … on feeling offended, shocked and uncomfortable following interactions with Mr Edwards”.

Current and former staff at the ICO told Computer Weekly in July that it was “inconceivable” that senior leaders at the organisation, including current chief executive Paul Arnold, were unaware of Edwards’ misconduct.

“There isn’t enough challenge at the top [within the senior leadership team], and there isn’t enough psychological safety among the middle and more junior levels to challenge upwards,” one staff member said, speaking under conditions of anonymity.

Another well-placed anonymous source said: “There’s also a sincerely held belief that complaints about John’s behaviour were not taken forward as they should have been.”

Ken Macdonald, former head of ICO Regions, wrote in a post on LinkedIn today that he was concerned the review is expected to report back by the first quarter of 2027, questioning whether that would leave enough time.

“I fear that’s rather optimistic given the extent of the bullying behaviours which I have been made aware of from some of my former colleagues,” he said. “If proven true … the previous commissioner’s behaviour will be the least of the new commission’s worries.”

Unions campaigned for wider review

The review follows a campaign by staff and trade unions to expand a more limited investigation proposed by the ICO that would have been run internally by the organisation and would have excluded former staff from giving evidence.

The PCS said it had pressed for significant changes, including the appointment of an independent barrister, arrangements for former staff to speak and the ability of the review to scrutinise decisions by managers, following a campaign and a day of action.

General secretary Fran Heathcote said the review was a significant step in addressing longstanding concerns by staff at the ICO. “The review must establish what has gone wrong and deliver meaningful recommendations for change,” she said. “Our members deserve a workplace where bullying and harassment are not tolerated, and nobody is afraid to speak up.”

Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, said the review would identify what is working, where things are falling short and what needs to change. “I want current and former staff to feel able to speak openly about their experiences and to know they will be taken seriously,” she said.

Paul Arnold, acting ICO chief executive, said: “While this has been an unsettling time for everyone at the ICO, establishing this independent review in the wake of the former commissioner’s resignation reflects our ongoing commitment to listening and learning from the events of the last year and those leading up to it.”

Former staff signed NDAs

The Information Commission has entered into 16 non-disclosure agreements with current or former members of staff at a cost of £354,000 since January 2020, according to disclosures under the Freedom of Information Act. Nine of the agreements included clauses to prevent employees making disparaging comments about their former employer.

Former technology secretary Kendall told the Science, Innovation and Technology Committee on 8 July that Edwards was “preparing to serve legal papers on one of the women at the ICO who raised concerns about his behaviour”.

  • 50% of respondents say they have been a victim of bullying, harassment and discrimination
  • 75% of respondents do not accept that ICO has a zero-tolerance approach to bullying, harassment and discrimination
  • Around 65% of respondents did not feel confident that complaints are investigated fairly by the ICO
  • 75% of respondents did not believe that perpetrators are held accountable for their actions
  • Only 7% of respondents said that instances of  of bullying, harassment and discrimination were decreasing whilst 93% believed instances were either staying the same or increasing.

title: Power now the binding constraint on AI datacentres
